q-85923.name: Question 1
q-85923.problem: Given that $A=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} & -3\end{aligned}],$ find the product of the eigenvalues of $A.$
q-85923.worked_solution:
The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & ={\lambda }^{2}-\text{tr}(A)\lambda +\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using Vieta's Formulas, we have that the roots of $p(\lambda ),$ i.e. the eigenvalues of $A,$ satisfy

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}+{\lambda }_{2}=\text{tr}(A) \\ {\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2}=\text{det}(A).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the product of the eigenvalues of $A$ is equal to the determinant of $A.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1}\cdot {\lambda }_{2} & =det(A) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}5 & 2\sqrt{5} \\ \sqrt{5} & -3\end{aligned}| \\  & =5\cdot (-3)-\sqrt{5}\cdot 2\sqrt{5} \\  & =-15-10 \\  & =-25.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ 2 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(-3-\lambda )-2) & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -8) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-2{\lambda }^{2}-11\lambda +24 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}-2{A}^{2}-11A+24I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}-2{A}^{2}-11A+24I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}-2A-11I+24{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 24{A}^{-1} & =11I+2A-{A}^{2} \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{11}{24}I+\frac{1}{12}A-\frac{1}{24}{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

q-85928.problem: Given that $\,A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{A}^{-1}=pI+qA$, find the value $p+q.$
q-85928.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2}-7A+8I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{2}-7A+8I) & =O \\ A-7I+8{A}^{-1} & =O \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{8}I-\frac{1}{8}A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=\frac{7}{8},$ $q=-\frac{1}{8}$ and

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{8}+(-\frac{1}{8})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 3 \\ -4 & 5-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(5-\lambda )+12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +22 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
p+q=\frac{7}{22}+(-\frac{1}{22})=\frac{3}{11}.

$\,\,{x}^{20}$
${x}^{2}-1\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{22}\,-\,{x}^{20}\,+\,3x\,-\,2\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{22}$ $-$ ${x}^{20}$

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(3x-2)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{20}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(3A-2I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(3A-2I) \\ & =3A-2I \\ & =3[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -6 \\ 12 & -9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}7 & -6 \\ 12 & -11\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda ):$ $$ \begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\ & =|\begin{aligned}4-\lambda & 2 \\ -6 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\ & =(4-\lambda )(-4-\lambda )+12 \\ & ={\lambda }^{2}-4\end{aligned} $$ Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:
$\,\,{x}^{14}$
${x}^{2}-4\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{16}\,-\,4{x}^{14}\,+\,7x\,-\,3\phantom{|}}$
${x}^{16}$ $-$ $4{x}^{14}$
$7x$ $-$ $3$
Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as $$ \begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\ & =q(x)p(x)+(7x-3)\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)={x}^{14}.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I). $$ According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(7A-3I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(7A-3I) \\ & =7A-3I \\ & =7[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ -6 & -4\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 14 \\ -42 & -28\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 14 \\ -42 & -31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned} $$

First, let's divide the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}$ by characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}-x-20,$ using long division:
$\,\,x$ $+$ $1$
${x}^{2}-x-20\,$ $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{3}\phantom{|}\,\,}$
${x}^{3}$ $-$ ${x}^{2}$ $-$ $20x$
${x}^{2}$ $+$ $20x$
${x}^{2}$ $-$ $x$ $-$ $20$
$21x$ $+$ $20$
Therefore, we can write ${x}^{3}$ as $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =q(x)p(x)+(21x+20),\end{aligned} $$ where $q(x)=x+1.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have $$ {A}^{3}=q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I). $$ Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & =q(A)p(A)+(21A+20I) \\ & =q(A)\cdot O+(21A+20I) \\ & =21A+20I.\end{aligned} $$
